Study 5's preregistered target was 125 participants, from simulations (simr; Green & MacLeod, 2016) using Study 4 as pilot data (α = .05/8; the weakest preregistered test reached 86% power), or 147 allowing for 15% attrition. table.research_questions:
Inferential Hypotheses:
1)	Correlation between Task A and Task B? 
H1: Task A and Task B minimum rate change scores will be positively correlated.
 
2)	Correlation Between Tasks and MAIA Scores? 
H2A: There will be a negative correlation between Minimum Rate Change and MAIA Total score

H2B: Task type will not moderate the correlation between minimum rate change and MAIA total score.

Explore: Can also explore MAIA correlations with other metrics such as overall accuracy. 

3)	Confidence scores? 
H3A: Main effect of Detection Accuracy on confidence, such that there will be higher confidence on trials in which change detection was accurate.  

H3B: Task type will not moderate the effect of accuracy on confidence.

4) Subjective Arousal?
H4A: Arousal will be predicted by Change Rate moderated by Accuracy
H4B: Task type will not moderate the moderation of change rate on arousal by accuracy (3 way interaction)

Explore: Arousal will be best predicted by Change Rate moderated by Confidence.

General Exploratory

E2. How much variance in minimum rate change is there in the two tasks? Do they each allow for a normal distribution of scores?

table.study_design_overview:
Within-Subjects Design. All participants will complete 2 Breathing Tasks measuring Interoceptive Awareness (Task A & Task B), subjective confidence and arousal questions following each trial, and a MAIA questionnaire.  Order of performing Task A and Task B will be counterbalanced across participants. 

Task A:  In this task participants will be asked to match their breath to a circle on a computer screen that expands and contracts rhythmically. Pulse rate will always start at 5-seconds/pulse. Participants will also be asked to indicate through a key press the beginning of every inhale and exhale. This offers a behavioral measure that indicates their ability to match their breathing rate with the pulsing circle. Each trial will consist of 8- circle pulses. As discovered in a previous pilot study (Farb & Logie, 2018) if the pulse of the circle is changed gradually with each breath, on average participants awareness of respiration change is no greater than chance levels even when the overall change is as large as 65% from initial breathing rate. Awareness of change is determined through a 3-way forced choice question after each trial (“On the previous trial did your breathing rate increase, decrease, or stay constant?”). For the current study, we are interested in calculating a threshold of awareness of change in respiration. To do so, a staircase method will be used, such that the overall change in respiration rate over the full trial will either increase or decrease (using a 1-up, 2-down rule) based upon correct or incorrect response on the previous trial. 2 correct responses in a row will lead to a step down in the staircase while 1 incorrect response will lead to one step easier. Step sizes represent total increase or decrease in respiration rate from the previous position on the staircase. The first level of overall respiration rate change will be 50% over the 8 pulses. Speed-up, Slow-down as well as “no-change” trials will be used [1/3 of total trials for each] so that the pulse rate is not changing every time. 

Task B. In this task participants will also match their breath to a circle on a computer screen that expands and contracts rhythmically. Pulse rate will always start at 5-seconds/pulse. Participants will also be asked to indicate through a key press when they begin each inhale and exhale. However in this task participants will be asked to press the spacebar once they notice that their breathing rate has changed.  “No change” trials, in which the rate of the pulses stays constant the entire duration of the trial, will be randomly interspersed so that the pulse rate is not changing every time. In total there will be 4 “no-change”, 4 speed-up and 4 slow-down trials randomly presented. The maximum number of pulses for each trial will be capped at 12.

table.stopping_rule:
We will post participant sign-up slots by week on the preceding Friday night, with 20 spots posted per week. We will post 20 new slots each week if, on that Friday night, we are below 320 participants.
We will post an initial 10 participants and review that data is logging correctly and that there are no major technical issues. We will then collect an additional 150 through the Prolific database, and allow up to 180 participants through the University of Toronto Participant Pool. We anticipate that the Prolific pool will complete rapidly, and at that time we will review participant adherence (>70% circle accuracy tracking  on 80% (12 of 15) trials in each version of the study, completion of all study elements). At that time we will compute how many participants are lacking to get to a full 180 and recruit the remaining participants in an additional wave of prolific recruitment. If the UofT pool reaches 180, a similar review will be performed, although based on past studies we do not anticipate this will happen- the UofT pool will be retained at whatever sample size is acquired by the pool’s closing at the end of the academic term.

table.study_design_overview:
Study Design:
The purpose of the study is to validate a novel task for measuring individual differences in breath awareness, specifically the ability to detect changes in breathing rate and the confidence associated with detection judgments. The study is mostly a within-participant design, featuring the Breath Change Awareness Task (BCAT), a heartbeat counting task, and self-questionnaires assessing interoceptive awareness, self-confidence, and subjective well-being. 

Participants will attend a single 1 hour laboratory session, in which they will complete informed consent and be outfitted with respiration and heartbeat monitors. They will then perform the BCAT, the heartbeat counting task, self-report questionnaires, and then the BCAT again to assess test-retest reliability.

The BCAT features a learning phase that has two main factors: (1) direction/magnitude of respiratory change [faster/slower/no change], and (2) the salience of the change [high/low]. Following each BCAT paced breathing trial (see materials for details), participants will engage in a three-alternative forced choice around change detection. The magnitude of change will be determined by a psychophysics staircase to estimate participant’s ability to detect change in respiration rate. The BCAT then features a testing phase in which participants will be assessed at their high salience threshold while manipulating trial salience to verify whether the participant thresholds have been correctly estimated. 

Between-Participant Randomization: to determine the extent to which task performance can be explained by visual detection alone, participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions: visual and breath. In the [breath] condition participants will receive normal BCAT instructions before each of the BCAT tasks; in the [visual] condition, participants will first be instructed only to view the circle’s changing rate, with no reference to the breath; then, upon the repetition of the BCAT, all participants will be told to breath along with the circle and join their breath.

Within-Participant Randomization: the BCAT features within participant randomization as the order of the 4 different staircase conditions (deceleration low salience, deceleration high salience, acceleration low salience, acceleration high salience) will be counterbalanced randomly by participant. table.manipulated_variables:
Group (between subjects): participants will be randomly assigned to either first perform the experimental task using vision alone (visual) or breathing along with the circle (breath). All participants will do the breath version when they repeat the task.

Magnitude of Respiratory Change (within subjects): degree of variation in breathing rate that occurs between consecutive trials, relevant in differentiating between high or low salience conditions.

Salience (within subjects): noticeability of the change in breathing rate, making it easier or harder for a participant to detect, i.e. how perceptible or striking the change in breathing rate is to the participant.
table.measured_variables:
Breath Change Awareness Task. A three-alternative forced choice task that employs a psychophysics staircase to estimate participant’s ability to detect change in respiration rate. 

Training Trials: Participants are presented with trials in which their breathing rate either increases or decreases over four breaths, with changes occurring either gradually or quickly. After each trial, participants are asked to identify whether their breathing rate increased or decreased, rate their confidence in the accuracy of their response, and report their level of wakefulness or arousal. Four distinct conditions are used: high salience (rapid changes) and low salience (gradual changes) for both acceleration and deceleration of breathing. 

For high salience trials, the change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration in a single multiplication between pulse 2 and 3: New duration = Old Duration * Change Amount

For low salience trials, the local (pulse specific) change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration between every pulse using the following calculation:
LocalChange= ChangeAmount ^ 1/(numBreaths -1) 

Test trials: Following the staircase for the four conditions, the high salience thresholds will be used for 16 test trials. The test trials will evenly split direction type: i.e., they will consist of 8 acceleration and 8 deceleration trials. Within each direction, there will be 4 high salience and 4 low salience trials. However, the threshold will be set consistently at the high salience threshold for that direction across all 8 trials. We would therefore expect accuracy to decrease for low salience trials as generally the high salience threshold will be too difficult to detect in a low salience trial presentation.

Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether the breathing rate has increased or decreased after each trial by comparing their response to the actual change that occurred. 

Confidence: the self-reported certainty a participant has in their assessment of whether the breathing rate increased or decreased after each trial.

Arousal: self-reported level of alertness after each trial to capture the subjective experience of perceived difficulty or the extent to which the change in breathing rate captured their attention.

Stress. The Brief Inventory of Perceived Stress (BIPS; Lehman et al., 2012) is a 9 item questionnaire that assesses stress across three dimensions: lack of control, conflict and imposition, and pushed (3 questions per subscale). The questionnaire items are rated on a 5-point scale (0 = Never, 4 = Very Often) similar to the two stress questionnaires - Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) and Perceived Stress Questionnaire (PSQ) - BIPS is derived from. At the 1-month and 1-year mark, the BIPS test-retest reliabilities were comparable to those of the PSS. 
DOI: 10.1002/jclp.21843
Lehman, K. A., Burns, M. N., Gagen, E. C., & Mohr, D. C. (2012). Development of the Brief Inventory of Perceived Stress. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 68(6), 631–644. https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.21843

Graphic emoji ratings: Created by Norman Farb, PhD to assess 4 measures - alertness (tired - wired), sad - happy, relaxed - stressed, and life satisfaction - on a 6-point scale. The emoticons are unvalidated but used as experimental quick assessment measures. 

Pos and Negative Emotion / Mood. The Scale of Positive and Negative Experience (SPANE; Diener et al., 2009) is a 12-item brief scale measuring positive and negative experiences (6-items each, scored separately) based on the frequency of feelings during the past month. Each item is rated on a scale from 1-5 (1 = Very Rarely or Never, 5 = Very Often or Always), with summed scores ranging from 6 to 30. Subtracting the negative score from the positive score results in the combined score which can range from -24 to 24.
Diener, E., Wirtz, D., Biswas-Diener, R., Tov, W., Kim-Prieto, C., Choi, D., & Oishi, S. (2009). New Measures of Well-Being. In Assessing Well-Being (pp. 247–266). Springer Netherlands. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-90-481-2354-4_12

Research indicates that single-item measures perform comparably to the SWLS in assessing life satisfaction, demonstrating similar correlations with external variables such as health and affect, and producing consistent conclusions about life satisfaction across different samples.

Items are rated on a 7-point scale from 1 (= Not at all) to 7 (= Very much) for items measuring intensity and 1 (= Never) to 7 (= Very much) for items measuring frequency. Correlations were made with Big Five Personality Traits - measured using the Big Five Inventory (BFI) - and latent factor models revealed satisfactory to excellent model fit (CFI = .991, RMSEA = .036).

Alexithymia (Perth)
The Perth Alexithymia Questionnaire-Short Form (PAQ-S; Preece et al., 2023) is a brief, 6-item measure designed to assess alexithymia, a trait involving difficulties with recognizing and articulating emotions, and a tendency to focus on external events over internal experiences. The questionnaire has 2-items per the three core dimensions: difficulty identifying feelings (DIF), difficulty describing feelings (DDF), and externally oriented thinking (EOT). Items are rated on a 7-point scale, with higher scores reflecting greater alexithymic traits. Additionally, the PAQ-S is designed to balance positively and negatively worded items, ensuring a comprehensive and nuanced evaluation of alexithymia.

Personality
The Big Five Inventory-10 (BFI-10; Rammstedt & John, 2007) is a shortened measure of the Big Five personality traits, developed as an abbreviated version from the BFI-44. It consists of 10-items, 2-items representing each of the five personality dimensions: extraversion, conscientiousness, neuroticism, agreeableness, and openness. The BFI-10 contains less than 25% of the items in the full BFI-44 yet retains strong predictive validity, capturing approximately 70% of the variance of the original measure. Test-retest analyses indicate that extraversion, conscientiousness, and neuroticism demonstrate higher stability over time, whereas agreeableness and openness exhibit slightly lower stability. Items are rated on a 5-point scale, ranging from 1 (= disagree strongly) to 5 (= agree strongly).


Demographics
The demographic questionnaire collects information on participants’ background, including age, year of study, gender identity, and self-identification with Indigenous, racial, or ethnocultural groups. table.indices:
Group: the between group assignment to do the first BCAT normally (Breath condition), or as a visual control condition, to be instructed only to view the circle’s changing rate, with no reference to the breath; then, upon the repetition of the BCAT, participants will be told to breath along with the circle and join their breath (Visual condition).

Detection Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether their breathing accelerated or decelerated after each trial compared to the actual change that occurred. 

Direction: whether a given trial involves acceleration or deceleration of the respiratory rate. A -1 indicates acceleration, and a 1 indicates deceleration

Level: the proportion change in the circle pulse duration from the start to the end of the trial. For example a 30% acceleration or deceleration is a level of .3

Magnitude of Respiratory Change: the degree of variation in the breathing rate, specifically the extent of acceleration and deceleration, observed across trials. This measures how large or significant the change in breathing rate is as determined by the psychophysical staircase method, which adjusts based on the participant’s correct or incorrect assessment of whether their breathing rate has increased or decreased. It is formally calculated as Direction * Level, so an acceleration of 30% = -1 * .3 = -.3, where as a deceleration of 30% = 1 * .3 = .3; this allows for the total change amount to be calculated as 1 + the magnitude of change.

Salience: how easily noticeable the change in breathing rate is after each trial. Either a gradual change in breathing rate (low salience) or marked change in breathing rate (high salience). 

Threshold: the minimum change in respiratory acceleration or deceleration required for a participant to reliably detect a shift in breathing rate. This threshold is determined using a psychophysical staircase procedure, where stimulus intensity is adaptively adjusted based on performance. A lower threshold indicates greater sensitivity, indicating that a participant can detect smaller changes in breathing rates, whereas a higher threshold suggests reduced sensitivity, requiring larger changes for detection. This measure serves as an index of interoceptive precision in the context of respiratory perception. The threshold score is calculated as the average of the last 2 trials in the staircase for any given condition.

Arousal: a participant’s self-reported level of emotional activation in response to each breathing rate trial. Arousal is assessed using a 6-point graphic rating scale featuring emoji representations, allowing participants to gauge their internal state. This measure captures an individual’s perceived intensity of arousal in response to changes in breathing rate.

Confidence: a participant’s self-assessed certainty in their judgement of whether the breathing rate accelerated or decelerated during a given trial. Confidence is measured using a 6-point numeric scale, with higher ratings indicating greater certainty in the accuracy of their response. This measure provides insight into a participants’ meta-perceptual awareness, reflecting their ability to evaluate the reliability of their interoceptive judgements. 

Adaptive Interoception: an individual’s ability to accurately perceive and interpret internal bodily sensations in a way that supports effective self-regulation and well-being. It reflects the capacity to detect and differentiate between accelerations and decelerations in breathing rate. Sensitivity to internal physiological changes is indicative of refined interoceptive awareness, allowing individuals to appropriately respond to bodily cues and adjust their physiological or emotional states accordingly.

table.exploratory_analyses:
The main exploratory analyses will look at differences in task performance between the visual and breath versions of the task, especially around test-retest reliability, where we expect the overall reliability to be numerically lower (but not appropriate for inferences). We also have many different questionnaires for wellbeing and interoception that will serve as exploratory/explanatory variables but are not central to the study research questions.

The relationship between the BCAT scores and other measures (most questionnaire scores and the heartbeat counting task) that are not specified in the main hypotheses will be considered exploratory analyses and not grounds for statistical inference. 

We will specifically explore whether controlling for some of our focal analyses, especially the relationship between task confidence and MAIA scores, is explained by questionnaires such as more general self-esteem / self-confidence, but these analyses are designed to rule out confounding explanations rather than to be the subject of investigation themselves.

Training Trials: Participants are presented with trials in which their breathing rate either increases or decreases over four breaths, with changes occurring either gradually or quickly. After each trial, participants are asked to identify whether their breathing rate increased or decreased, rate their confidence in the accuracy of their response, and report their level of wakefulness or arousal. Four distinct conditions are used: high salience (rapid changes) and low salience (gradual changes) for both acceleration and deceleration of breathing.

For high salience trials, the change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration in a single multiplication between pulse 2 and 3: New duration = Old Duration * Change Amount

The test trials will evenly split direction type: i.e., they will consist of 8 acceleration and 8 deceleration trials. Within each direction, there will be 4 high salience and 4 low salience trials. However, the threshold will be set consistently at the high salience threshold for that direction across all 8 trials. We would therefore expect accuracy to decrease for low salience trials as generally the high salience threshold will be too difficult to detect in a low salience trial presentation.

Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether the breathing rate has increased or decreased after each trial by comparing their response to the actual change that occurred.

Confidence: the self-reported certainty a participant has in their assessment of whether the breathing rate increased or decreased after each trial.

Arousal: self-reported level of alertness after each trial to capture the subjective experience of perceived difficulty or the extent to which the change in breathing rate captured their attention.

Personality
The Big Five Inventory-10 (BFI-10; Rammstedt & John, 2007) is a shortened measure of the Big Five personality traits, developed as an abbreviated version from the BFI-44. It consists of 10-items, 2-items representing each of the five personality dimensions: extraversion, conscientiousness, neuroticism, agreeableness, and openness. The BFI-10 contains less than 25% of the items in the full BFI-44 yet retains strong predictive validity, capturing approximately 70% of the variance of the original measure. Detection Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether their breathing accelerated or decelerated after each trial compared to the actual change that occurred.

Direction: whether a given trial involves acceleration or deceleration of the respiratory rate. A -1 indicates acceleration, and a 1 indicates deceleration

Level: the proportion change in the circle pulse duration from the start to the end of the trial. For example a 30% acceleration or deceleration is a level of .3

Magnitude of Respiratory Change: the degree of variation in the breathing rate, specifically the extent of acceleration and deceleration, observed across trials. This measures how large or significant the change in breathing rate is as determined by the psychophysical staircase method, which adjusts based on the participant’s correct or incorrect assessment of whether their breathing rate has increased or decreased. It is formally calculated as Direction * Level, so an acceleration of 30% = -1 * .3 = -.3, where as a deceleration of 30% = 1 * .3 = .3; this allows for the total change amount to be calculated as 1 + the magnitude of change.

Salience: how easily noticeable the change in breathing rate is after each trial. Either a gradual change in breathing rate (low salience) or marked change in breathing rate (high salience).

Threshold: the minimum change in respiratory acceleration or deceleration required for a participant to reliably detect a shift in breathing rate. This threshold is determined using a psychophysical staircase procedure, where stimulus intensity is adaptively adjusted based on performance. A lower threshold indicates greater sensitivity, indicating that a participant can detect smaller changes in breathing rates, whereas a higher threshold suggests reduced sensitivity, requiring larger changes for detection. This measure serves as an index of interoceptive precision in the context of respiratory perception. The threshold score is calculated as the average of the last 2 trials in the staircase for any given condition.

live_data_statements: After four development studies (Prolific adults and undergraduates, N = 579), we report a preregistered laboratory study (N = 206) with verified breathing.

Study 4: four direction × salience staircase runs of 10 trials, then 8 test trials at fixed change sizes, before which all participants were asked to breathe along.

Study 1's preregistered target of 180 Prolific participants came from a simulation giving 97% power, at a Bonferroni-corrected α of .05/7, for the Change × Accuracy interaction on arousal.
Participants completed two BCAT versions in a single session (about 45 min), in counterbalanced order.
Study 2 (online, Prolific; N = 166 of 199 who began).
To continue, participants had to select the description matching their instruction.
Nine participants restarted the survey and were randomized to the other condition on one attempt; all are analyzed by the condition of the attempt that opened the task (Breath 63, Visual 68).
After Block 1, participants completed a heartbeat-counting task (Schandry, 1981).
In Studies 1 and 2 (Prolific, one submission per account), procedures were in place that screen out automated responding, although they were designed to check task compliance.
We used no CAPTCHA or IP filtering; every participant signed up through a registered account, on Prolific (Studies 1-2) or the university's Sona participant pool (Study 4).
All studies drew from convenience samples (Prolific or undergraduate pools); effect magnitudes may not generalize to other populations or to paces outside the range tested.

text.text: Does bodily change shape self-reported arousal only when it is noticed?
In the Breath Change Awareness Task, participants breathe with a visual pacer or follow it by vision alone, report whether its pace changed, and rate arousal.
After four development studies (Prolific adults and undergraduates, N = 579), we report a preregistered laboratory study (N = 206) with verified breathing.
Arousal followed noticed changes more steeply than missed ones, with or without breathing, and in most studies noticed effects scaled with a change's size beyond the reported direction.

In Study 5, missed changes moved arousal up to a third as much although breathing tracked the pacer closely, and a noticed breathed change moved arousal 1.8 [1.3, 2.7] times as much as one followed by vision alone, though not detectably in the online Study 4.
Ratings partly followed the preceding detection report.
Self-reported arousal mainly follows noticing; breathing adds to it. from the moderate position, part of it: the direction but not the size.

Because all three concern bodily change, they predict these effects only when the change is breathed, and a breathed change should move arousal more than an equally large one followed by vision alone (preregistered as a steeper change-arousal slope in the breathing group, H4C); the comparison of noticed changes at the same report and size is exploratory.
Table S17 in Section S17.5 lists every preregistered test.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S17</ref> in Section S17.5 lists every preregistered test.

text.text: A non-interoceptive account, in which the rating follows the report, predicts a noticing effect (a steeper change-arousal slope when a change is noticed) even from vision alone, but little effect of change magnitude on arousal.
Your breathing quickens, and you feel on edge.
Would the change have moved you if you had not noticed it?

Interoceptive signals, including heart rate, respiration, and visceral activity, are continuously integrated with cognitive and affective systems to produce feeling states (Craig, 2002; Sherrington, 1906), but whether a bodily change shapes feeling only when consciously perceived is unclear.
text.formatted: Interoceptive signals, including heart rate, respiration, and visceral activity, are continuously integrated with cognitive and affective systems to produce feeling states <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Craig, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sherrington, 1906)</ref>, but whether a bodily change shapes feeling only when consciously perceived is unclear.

text.text: Three theoretical positions give different answers.
The constitutive position holds that awareness is what makes bodily change felt.
James and Lange proposed that emotion is literally the perception of bodily change (James, 1884; Lange, 1885 Lange, /1912)).
text.formatted: James and Lange proposed that emotion is literally the perception of bodily change <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(James, 1884;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lange, 1885</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Lange, /1912))</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary work on interoceptive accuracy is consistent with this view: people who detect their heartbeat more accurately have been reported to rate emotional pictures as more arousing, but not as more pleasant or unpleasant (Pollatos et al., 2007), and their heart-rate reactions track their arousal ratings more closely (Dunn et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Contemporary work on interoceptive accuracy is consistent with this view: people who detect their heartbeat more accurately have been reported to rate emotional pictures as more arousing, but not as more pleasant or unpleasant <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pollatos et al., 2007)</ref>, and their heart-rate reactions track their arousal ratings more closely <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dunn et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, the constructivist position holds that arousal shapes affect without conscious access to the physiological signal.

Excitation transfer paradigms show that residual sympathetic activation amplifies emotional responses in proportion to its magnitude even when attributed to an irrelevant source (Zillmann, 1983), and subliminal threat paradigms show that skin conductance scales with threat level prior to conscious recognition (Öhman & Mineka, 2001).

text.text: Contemporary accounts propose that bodily signals shape affect continuously and before awareness, which follows as a product rather than a prerequisite (LeDoux & Brown, 2017; Seth, 2013; Winkielman & Berridge, 2004).

text.text: From this view, arousal magnitude transfers to subjective experience regardless of whether a physiological change crosses the detection threshold.

The moderate position allows arousal to transfer without awareness of its source, but still requires detection of some undifferentiated activation before it can be labeled. Schachter and Singer (1962) proposed that emotion requires two components: physiological arousal and a cognitive label borrowed from context.

text.text: The moderate position predicts that detection amplifies rather than enables feeling: undetected physiological change may impact subjective arousal, but only noticed changes carry magnitude information.
The three positions have rarely been tested directly, because few paradigms compare noticed and missed changes of the same size in a physiological signal within person and session.

Individual-differences approaches comparing people high versus low in interoceptive accuracy establish between-person associations but cannot produce within-person variation in awareness for the same physiological event (Dunn et al., 2010; Murphy et al., 2020).

text.text: The Breath Change Awareness Task (BCAT) was built to compare noticed and missed changes of the same size within person.
We report five studies, in which participants breathed with a pacing circle whose rate changed, abruptly or gradually, or stayed the same.
After each trial, they reported whether the pace had changed, then rated their confidence and arousal.
Because change size is set by the design while detection varies from trial to trial, each participant contributes both correctly noticed changes and missed ones, with unchanged trials as a baseline.
In Studies 4 and 5, a second group followed the pacer by vision alone, without breathing along; in Study 5, a breathing belt recorded respiration.
Although the pacing stimulus is visual, the BCAT targets the estimate of one's own breathing.
Exteroceptive and interoceptive signals routinely co-determine bodily self-models in everyday life (Quigley et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Exteroceptive and interoceptive signals routinely co-determine bodily self-models in everyday life <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Quigley et al., 2021</ref>).

text.text: An inference is interoceptive because of its target, here one's current breathing rate, not because it relies only on signals from inside the body (Schoeller et al., 2025).

text.text: Breathing along with the pacer adds an interoceptive source, the felt breath, to the visual one.
The BCAT can compare noticed and missed changes of a given size only if four things hold.
First, detection should rise with a change's size, so that changes near threshold are sometimes noticed and sometimes missed.
Second, abrupt changes should be detected at smaller sizes than gradual ones (preregistered as Study 5 H2), and more often at a fixed size (H5).
Third, breathing should follow the pacer on missed as well as noticed trials, so that a missed change is still a breathed change.
Fourth, participants who use vision alone should barely breathe along, so that the vision-alone condition removes the bodily change while keeping the visual one.

All three theoretical positions predict that a noticed change should move arousal in its direction, scaled with its size beyond the reported direction (among trials with the same report, larger changes should move arousal more).

Yet they differ on missed changes (preregistered as Study 5 H4A-B): from the constitutive position, a missed change should carry none of the response to a noticed one; from the constructivist position, all of it;

The 70% and 80% thresholds are heuristic.

Prevention and detection trade off here: the practice gate stops a respondent who does not follow the display before any data are collected, whereas the trial exclusions remove lapses afterwards and depend on where the threshold is set.

Trial-level heart rate could not serve as an independent index of arousal.

In breathing blocks, heart rate followed the pacing change, but in the opposite direction to rated arousal: it was higher after slowed than after sped-up pacing (0.86 beats per minute, bpm, per unit change [0.54, 1.19]).

When participants used vision alone, heart rate followed noticed changes (1.26 bpm per unit change [0.59, 1.94]) but not missed ones (-1.19 [-2.47, 0.10]), again in the opposite direction to the ratings.

It did not predict arousal ratings, either on its own or with the pacing change and the participant's measured breathing in the model (within person, -0.01 points per SD of heart-rate change [-0.03, 0.01]).
Adding heart rate and measured breathing left the difference between noticed and missed slopes unchanged in the breathing blocks (Section S6).

With vision alone the check is inconclusive: physiology could be aligned to trials for only 51 of the 111 participants, and in them the noticed-missed difference was near zero (-0.05 [-0.22, 0.12]) rather than the full group's -0.22 [-0.39, -0.06], so whether physiology accounts for the vision-alone effect is unknown (Section S6.3).

text.text: Speeding was the more consistent of the two.

None of the three positions survives as stated.
The constitutive position says a missed change is inert; it was not, though in Studies 3 and 5 the Bayes factors favored no missed direction effect (Table S14a).

text.text: The constructivist position says a missed change carries the whole response; it carried only a fraction, at best.
The moderate position gets the fraction right but assigns it to bodily change, and noticing mattered even when the change was seen but not breathed.
Noticed changes also carried their size.
The larger a noticed change, the more it moved arousal, with the reported direction and the participant's confidence held constant.
A rating that merely echoed the report could not do this: the report said which way the pace had changed, not by how much.
The scaling was clearest in Study 5, came mainly from speeding (Table S5b), and followed the change as presented rather than the breathing it produced.

text.text: Read together, the two effects say that most of the arousal response arrived with noticing, and that the size of the change then set how large it was; in Study 3, noticed changes also reached attractiveness ratings through arousal.
Felt arousal may draw on whatever signals a change in one's breathing: the seen pacer and, when breathing along, the felt breath, an interoceptive source (Quigley et al., 2021).

text.text: Noticing mattered regardless of which source carried the change, and breathing added to the response.
In Study 5, where breathing was verified, a noticed breathed change moved arousal about 1.8 times as much as an equally large change followed by vision alone (BF10 = 1.4).
Breathing added about as much to missed changes (interaction -0.03 [-0.23, 0.17]), though that addition was not itself reliable, so whether the interoceptive addition needs noticing is open.
If noticing drives what moves us, attention habits matter.
Speculatively, heightened attention to the body, as in panic disorder (Paulus & Stein, 2010), might raise felt arousal by bringing mild bodily changes to awareness.

text.text: What would matter is a habit of noticing rather than greater sensitivity.
Consistent with this, in a large community sample, mental-health symptoms tracked self-reported interoceptive sensibility but not measured interoceptive performance (Banellis et al., 2026).

text.text: Our only measure of felt arousal is a rating given after the detection judgment.
A rating that follows the report, or an appraisal of the noticed change, can therefore produce the noticing effect; the size effect rules out only a restated report.
Whether noticing changed how aroused participants felt, or only how they rated it, is open.

Influence may also have run the other way, with felt activation serving as evidence for the direction judgment: on unchanged trials, arousal was higher after "faster" than after "slower" reports in Study 4's breathing group (0.37 points [0.14, 0.59]) but not in Study 5 (Block 1, -0.02 [-0.28, 0.23]).

text.text: Part of the noticed-missed difference may thus reflect which trials were judged as changed rather than what noticing added.
On misses reported in the wrong direction, arousal leaned toward the report rather than the change, unlike misses reported "same" (difference 0.21 [0.02, 0.40]; Section S7.5).
Detection was measured rather than manipulated: the salience manipulation shifted it only modestly, which limits causal inference about the noticing effect.

Trial-level heart rate offered no independent check: with vision alone it responded to noticed but not to missed changes, in the direction of an orienting response rather than of the ratings (Section S6).
Rating arousal before the detection judgment, or measuring it outside the report, as with pupil size or skin conductance, would test these accounts directly.
Missed trials are not a random subset.
Detection depended on arousal before the trial, in opposite directions for slowing and speeding, and Study 4's staircases were blocked by direction.
The shares we report allow for the two preceding arousal ratings, but states that those ratings do not capture could still bias the shares either way.
Breathing along also changed how participants breathed.
The pacer imposed a 1:1 inhale:exhale rhythm, which participants adopted while breathing with it (the inhale took 47% of each paced breath, against 41% unpaced).
Breathing along thus differed from vision alone in rhythm, effort, proprioception and attention to the body as well as in interoceptive input.
Any of these could underlie the larger response to breathed changes, but none can explain the noticing or size effects, which appeared without breathing.
Because the pacer was always visible, the task never tests breath interoception on its own.
The arousal effects were small.

A typical noticed speeding (about 5-7 breaths per minute; Table S7a) raised arousal by 5-10% of the rating scale (breathing groups; Table 2), and the median participant used about half of the scale (42-60% across studies).

text.text: They arose near the detection threshold, from voluntary paced changes, in sessions over which arousal fell slightly, and may not extend to the large respiratory changes of strong emotion.
Test-retest reliability for individual threshold estimates fell short of the preregistered criterion of r ≥ .70 (Preregistered tests; Table S13g).

text.text: The ten-trial staircases were built to estimate group thresholds, not stable individual differences, and may require more trials to stabilize.
All studies drew from convenience samples (Prolific or undergraduate pools); effect magnitudes may not generalize to other populations or to paces outside the range tested.
Across five studies, the arousal response to a pacer change occurred mainly when the change was noticed, and in most studies a noticed change's size moved arousal beyond the reported direction.
Against the constitutive position, missed changes still moved arousal, though less steeply and less consistently than noticed ones.
Against the constructivist position, noticing mattered, even with vision alone.

Breathing along added an interoceptive source: a noticed breathed change moved arousal about 1.8 times as much as one followed by vision alone, although the online Study 4 did not detect a difference.
Self-reported arousal mainly follows noticing a change; an interoceptive source adds to it.
